units.title: Unit 11 — Describing character
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 11. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe character and personality with natural positive, negative, and neutral adjectives.
Use reliability, confidence, patience, hard work, and humour vocabulary accurately.
Recognise opposite pairs and negative prefixes un-, im-, and dis-.
Distinguish kind from nice, friendly, and pleasant, and sensible from clever or intelligent.
Describe friends using trust, creative, talented, talent, and wish.
Ask What is someone like? to enquire about character rather than physical appearance.

items.example: Her cheerful character makes her easy to work with.
items.note: Here character means the qualities that describe what a person is like.

items.example: Maya stays positive even when things go wrong.
items.note: A positive person expects good things or notices the good side of a situation.

items.example: He is negative about every suggestion we make.
items.note: A negative person often expects bad things or focuses on problems.

items.example: We need a reliable person to organise the event.
items.note: Someone reliable does what they say they will do.

items.pt: pouco confiável; em quem não se pode confiar
items.example: The bus service is unreliable, so I leave early.
items.note: The opposite of reliable; someone or something cannot be depended on.

items.example: I feel more confident when I have prepared well.
items.note: Confident people believe in their own abilities; not the same as arrogant.

items.example: She was shy when she met her new colleagues.
items.note: Someone shy is uncomfortable about speaking to unfamiliar people.

items.example: Our hard-working team finished the job early.
items.note: Describes a person who puts considerable effort into work or study.

items.example: I feel lazy on Sunday mornings.
items.note: The opposite of hard-working in this unit; someone who avoids effort.

items.example: She has a great sense of humour and makes us laugh.
items.note: The ability to notice and enjoy funny things; usually have a good sense of humour.

items.example: He seems serious at first, but he likes jokes.
items.note: About character, someone serious is often quiet or does not laugh much.

items.example: Our teacher is patient when students make mistakes.
items.note: Able to wait calmly and avoid becoming angry.

items.example: The children became impatient while waiting for the bus.
items.note: The opposite of patient; im- is the negative prefix in this word.

items.example: What's he like as a colleague?
items.note: Ask this about character; use What does he look like? for appearance.

items.example: What are you like when you are under pressure?
items.note: A question about character or behaviour, not a request for a physical description.

items.example: He's quite shy until he gets to know people.
items.note: Quite changes the degree of an adjective; its strength can depend on context.

items.example: My neighbour was generous with her time.
items.note: Willing to give help, time, or money to others.

items.example: He is too mean to share the cost of lunch.
items.note: Here mean means unwilling to give money or help; it can also mean unkind in other contexts.

items.example: Please be honest about what happened.
items.note: An honest person tells the truth; h is silent.

items.example: It would be dishonest to say you wrote the report yourself.
items.note: The opposite of honest, formed with dis-.

items.example: That was a clever way to solve the problem.
items.note: Able to understand things or think of solutions quickly.

items.example: The students asked intelligent questions.
items.note: Good at understanding and learning; similar to clever in this unit.

items.example: It was a stupid mistake, but we fixed it.
items.note: An informal, potentially insulting judgement; describe an action rather than a person when possible.

items.example: She stayed calm during the emergency.
items.note: Not worried, upset, or easily frightened; l is silent.

items.example: I get nervous before important meetings.
items.note: Worried or uneasy, especially before an event.

items.example: He felt anxious about the results.
items.note: Often worried about a possible problem or future event.

items.example: It was kind of you to help the visitor.
items.note: A kind person wants to help others; compare nice, friendly and pleasant.

items.example: That was an unkind thing to say.
items.note: The opposite of kind; un- creates the negative form.

items.example: Our new neighbour seems very nice.
items.note: A general positive adjective for pleasant people or experiences.

items.example: The receptionist was friendly to everyone.
items.note: Someone friendly is warm and happy to speak to people.

items.example: The new manager sounded unfriendly on the phone.
items.note: The opposite of friendly; un- is a negative prefix.

items.example: We had a pleasant conversation after class.
items.note: Enjoyable or polite; a person described as pleasant is agreeable to others.

items.example: He was unpleasant to the waiter.
items.note: The opposite of pleasant; un- is a negative prefix.

items.example: Choosing to rest was a sensible decision.
items.note: Practical and able to make good decisions; not the same as sensitive.

items.example: We laughed about a silly mistake.
items.note: Not sensible or a little foolish; can also mean playful rather than unintelligent.

items.example: I trust Nina to keep a secret.
items.note: Believe that someone is honest and dependable; trust someone, not trust in someone in this everyday use.

items.example: She's creative and enjoys finding new solutions.
items.note: Able to think of original ideas or make new things.

items.example: He's a talented young musician.
items.note: Having a natural ability to do something particularly well.

items.example: She has a talent for learning languages.
items.note: A natural ability; often have a talent for something.

items.example: I wish I had more time for painting.
items.note: I wish + past form expresses an unreal present situation or something you would like to change.

items.example: Her practical advice helped us choose a better option.
items.note: In the exercise, being practical is part of being sensible.

items.example: Use your imagination to design a new game.
items.note: The ability to think of new ideas or pictures in your mind; relevant to creative.

items.example: He finds it hard to talk to strangers.
items.note: A person whom you do not know; used in the exercise about being shy.

items.example: Please be patient with the new students.
items.note: Use patient with someone and patient about something; the adjective takes the preposition with for people.

items.example: I trust my colleagues to meet the deadline.
items.note: Trust is followed directly by a person as object; no preposition is needed.

items.example: She's good at thinking of new ideas.
items.note: Use good at + noun or -ing form to describe an ability.

units.title: Unit 12 — Feelings
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 12. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify emotional adjectives and distinguish character traits from temporary feelings.
Use emotion, feelings and emotional accurately, including the plural noun feelings.
Associate proud, disappointed, jealous, confused, curious and anxious with their related nouns.
Describe being scared, frightened, upset, cheerful, miserable or depressed in everyday contexts.
Explain how weather and colour can affect mood, energy levels and stress.
Use patterns such as proud of, disappointed with, anxious about, care for and have an effect on.

items.example: Music can create a strong emotion.
items.note: An emotion is a feeling such as love, fear, or anger.

items.example: I had a strange feeling before the interview.
items.note: Can mean an emotion or an impression; often appears in the plural when talking about emotions.

items.example: She finds it difficult to talk about her feelings.
items.note: Frequently plural when referring to a person's emotions.

items.example: He became emotional during the farewell speech.
items.note: Someone emotional shows feelings readily, or something can cause strong feelings.

items.example: Her parents are proud of her progress.
items.note: Pleased by your own achievements or those of someone close to you.

items.example: He took great pride in his work.
items.note: The noun related to proud; take pride in something.

items.example: I was disappointed with the final result.
items.note: Unhappy because something was not as good as you expected.

items.example: Missing the concert was a disappointment.
items.note: The noun related to disappointed.

items.example: I felt confused by the instructions.
items.note: Unable to understand or think clearly about a situation.

items.example: There was some confusion about the meeting time.
items.note: The noun related to confused.

items.example: We're hopeful that the repairs will be finished today.
items.note: Believing that something positive will happen in the future.

items.example: The children were curious about the new machine.
items.note: Wanting to learn or discover something.

items.example: Her curiosity led her to study astronomy.
items.note: The noun related to curious.

items.example: She was anxious about travelling alone.
items.note: Worried about something that might happen; related noun: anxiety.

items.example: He felt anxiety before the competition.
items.note: The noun related to anxious.

items.example: I was scared when I heard the loud noise.
items.note: Feeling afraid; similar in meaning to frightened.

items.example: She was frightened by the sudden crash.
items.note: Feeling afraid; a synonym of scared in this unit.

items.example: He felt jealous when his friend received all the attention.
items.note: An emotion associated with jealousy; in relationships, fear of losing someone's attention.

items.example: Jealousy can damage a relationship.
items.note: The noun related to jealous.

items.example: She was upset after the argument.
items.note: Unhappy because something unpleasant has happened.

items.example: He's cheerful even on rainy days.
items.note: Happy and positive in mood or manner.

items.example: I felt miserable when I had to stay home alone.
items.note: Extremely unhappy or uncomfortable.

items.example: She felt depressed throughout the long winter.
items.note: Describes feeling very unhappy and without hope; persistent symptoms can warrant professional help.

items.example: His mood improved after some rest.
items.note: The way someone feels at a particular time.

items.example: Seasonal affective disorder can occur during darker months.
items.note: A form of depression linked to seasonal patterns; often abbreviated SAD.

items.example: SAD can affect some people during winter.
items.note: In this unit SAD is an abbreviation for seasonal affective disorder; pronounced like the word sad.

items.example: Some people suffer from stress during examinations.
items.note: Used with an illness, condition, or other unpleasant experience.

items.example: I feel energetic after a good night's sleep.
items.note: Full of energy and wanting to be active.

items.example: She expressed her anger calmly.
items.note: The noun for the strong feeling of being angry.

items.example: He was angry about the unexpected delay.
items.note: Feeling strong displeasure; related noun: anger.

items.example: She showed maternal affection towards the baby.
items.note: Related to a mother or typical of a mother's care.

items.example: He's a caring friend who helps when someone is ill.
items.note: Describes someone who looks after other people and cares about them.

items.example: Too much stress can affect sleep.
items.note: Mental pressure or worry caused by difficult situations.

items.example: I find walking by the sea relaxing.
items.note: Something relaxing makes you feel calm; contrast with relaxed for how a person feels.

items.example: They came up with a creative solution.
items.note: Able to produce original ideas or use imagination.

items.example: He's proud of his team's achievements.
items.note: Use proud of a person, achievement, or event.

items.example: They were disappointed with the service.
items.note: Disappointed with something; disappointed that + clause also occurs.

items.example: I'm confused about which form to complete.
items.note: Use confused about a subject or situation.

items.example: She's curious about how the device works.
items.note: Use curious about something you want to understand.

items.example: They were anxious about the journey.
items.note: Use anxious about a future event or possible problem.

items.pt: com ciúmes de; com inveja de
items.example: He was jealous of his friend's success.
items.note: Use jealous of someone or something; the emotion may involve envy or relationships.

items.example: She's upset about what happened yesterday.
items.note: Use upset about a situation or event.

items.example: The weather can have an effect on my mood.
items.note: Use have an effect on someone or something; effect is a noun here.

items.example: Bright light can affect your mood.
items.note: Affect is the verb; effect is usually a noun in the pattern have an effect on.

items.example: Green is often associated with nature.
items.note: Use associated with to connect two things.

items.example: He helps care for his elderly grandfather.
items.note: Here care for means look after someone; care for can also mean like in other contexts.

items.example: She rarely shows her feelings at work.
items.note: Express your emotions visibly or openly.

items.example: Many workers suffer from stress at busy times.
items.note: Suffer from is followed by a condition or unpleasant experience.

items.example: Regular exercise had a good effect on her mood.
items.note: A noun for a change or result produced by something; have an effect on.

items.example: I hope the weather improves tomorrow.
items.note: The noun or verb related to hopeful; hope that + clause is common.

items.example: I sometimes feel scared when walking alone at night.
items.note: A natural pattern for saying someone is afraid.
